notes: Unusual permission to appeal on Hughes v Metropolitan Railway estoppel over GC35 variation procedure; facts and order are clear.

enrichment.short_title: North Sea Ventilation v Consafe: permission to appeal on GC35 estoppel
key_facts: Consafe subcontracted HVAC works to North Sea Ventilation under a fixed-price contract incorporating GC35 change procedures for a BNFL plutonium waste retrieval project.
The subcontractor claimed GC35 was varied or disapplied by a Hughes v Metropolitan Railway course of conduct involving oral instructions, variation orders and payment of about £400,000 in extras.
By August 2003 Consafe admitted a further £424,000 was due on variations but withheld payment pending set-off claims.
The judge found Consafe insisted on written proposals from October 2001, but the appellant argued the dispensing conduct continued thereafter.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal after refusal on the papers in a building contract preliminary issues trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted on the estoppel issue with a one-and-a-half to two day estimate before a three-judge court; fresh skeleton and clarified grounds ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where substantial payments were made on variation orders without insisting on GC35 compliance and the defendant later admitted further sums were due, there may be sufficient material to justify permission to appeal on whether a course of conduct dispensed with strict contractual change procedures, albeit the burden on the claimant remains heavy.
legal_issues: Whether a Hughes v Metropolitan Railway estoppel arose from oral instructions and payments on variation orders
Whether GC35 continued to apply after October 2001
Whether the judge misdirected on the burden of proof
Whether there was no case to answer at the close of the claimants' case
linked_authorities: Hughes v Metropolitan Railway Co (1877) 2 App Cas 439

confidence.notes: Interlocutory permission judgment; estoppel merits remain for full appeal.

notes: Section 288 TPO appeal on tree definition and dangerous tree arguments; Collins J dismissed with summary costs.

enrichment.short_title: Fowler v Ealing: challenge to tree preservation order at Grade II listed house
key_facts: Dr Fowler appealed against confirmation of a TPO covering nine trees at 134 Church Road, Hanwell, a Grade II listed building with a neglected garden.
He sought to fund restoration works partly by developing part of the garden and challenged inclusion of a diseased chestnut and two arbutus said to be shrubs not trees.
An inspector allowed removal of the chestnut after the Council refused consent; the Secretary of State rejected pollarding as sufficient.
The appellant also alleged council misfeasance arising from soured relations and a neighbour officer, but evidence was speculative.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 appeal to the Administrative Court against confirmation of a tree preservation order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on all grounds; costs summarily assessed at £3,500 rather than the £5,600 claimed.
enrichment.ratio: A council may rationally include a tree in a TPO where it reasonably considers the tree has sufficient life, even if diseased; 'tree' bears its ordinary meaning and arbutus may properly be so classified; misfeasance requires strong evidence not shown here.
legal_issues: Whether a dangerous or diseased tree may be included in a TPO under section 198(6)
Whether arbutus plants are trees or shrubs as a matter of law
Whether council misfeasance vitiated the order
Summary assessment of local authority costs

confidence.notes: Statutory interpretation, findings and costs order are all clearly recorded.

notes: Detailed section 288 challenge to inspector's refusal of UCL student block in Bloomsbury conservation area; Sullivan J dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: UCL v Secretary of State: conservation area challenge to Hertford Place student block

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: UCL sought to quash an inspector's dismissal of its appeal against non-determination of planning permission to demolish a two-storey office and erect a nine-floor student accommodation block at Hertford Place, Bloomsbury.
The inspector found the proposal would harm the courtyard environment, reduce openness visible from Whitfield Street and obscure evidence of the historic mews pattern.
The Council had indicated refusal on conservation area and urban design grounds; the scheme included 110 bedrooms and an under-fives day centre.
UCL argued the inspector wrongly treated private realm and streetscene harm as engaging section 72 and failed to balance need and benefits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 application to quash an inspector's decision on a non-determination planning appeal after an informal hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; all five grounds rejected; Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £4,632.
enrichment.ratio: Section 72(1) applies throughout a conservation area, not only where special architectural characteristics remain; harm to courtyard openness and glimpses through mews archways may properly engage conservation area duties; decision letters should not be subjected to excessively legalistic textual criticism.
legal_issues: Whether harm within a redeveloped courtyard was relevant under section 72(1)
Whether loss of historic street pattern was fairly raised at the hearing
Whether the inspector failed to balance student accommodation need against harm
Whether South Lakeland limits development objections to designated special qualities
linked_authorities: South Lakeland District Council v Secretary of State for the Environment [1992] 2 AC 141
Castleford Homes v Secretary of State for the Environment Transport and the Regions [2001] PLCR 470

confidence.notes: Long but coherent judgment resolving multiple linked planning grounds.

notes: Full Court appeal on guilty plea following bad advice and money laundering mens rea; conviction dismissed, sentence reduced.

enrichment.short_title: Saik: appeal against money laundering plea and seven-year sentence
key_facts: Saik managed the Sirafa Administration Bureau and pleaded guilty to conspiring to convert about $8m suspected criminal proceeds between December 2001 and February 2002.
He claimed erroneous advice on likely sentence and on protection of his matrimonial home in confiscation proceedings influenced his plea.
Counsel had relied on outdated Lee and Taigel authorities predating removal of judicial discretion under the 1995 Act amendments.
The Crown accepted a basis of actual suspicion rather than knowledge and a limited conspiracy period after negotiation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full Court appeal by leave against conviction and application for leave against a seven-year sentence after guilty plea at Kingston Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed and seven years replaced with five and a half years.
enrichment.ratio: Erroneous advice on sentence length or confiscation is ordinarily peripheral to a free guilty plea unless it goes to the heart of acknowledgment of guilt as in Turner; suspicion suffices for conspiracy to launder under section 93C(2) following Rizvi; post-1995 confiscation law removes discretion to spare matrimonial homes.
legal_issues: Whether bad advice on sentence or confiscation invalidated the guilty plea
Whether reasonable grounds for suspicion can found statutory conspiracy under section 1(2)
Whether the plea was to a non-existent offence
Whether seven years properly reflected the negotiated basis of plea
linked_authorities: R v Rizvi and Christi [2003] EWCA Crim 3575
R v Turner [1970] 54 Cr App R 352
R v Ahmed and Qureshi [2004] EWCA Crim 2599

confidence.notes: Detailed Full Court judgment on plea validity and sentencing hierarchy.

notes: Trust company director remuneration summary judgment reversed; Carnwath LJ remitted for trial on service agreement validity.

enrichment.short_title: Thane Investments v Tomlinson: director service agreements remitted for trial
key_facts: Discretionary trust companies Thane Investments and Denbrae held funds settled in 1965; Mr Tomlinson was a long-serving director and trustee.
In 1997 service agreements paying Tomlinson £50,000 and Knopp lesser sums were approved at board meetings where each abstained on his own contract.
The companies claimed the agreements were void for lack of shareholder approval and sought repayment including sums paid to Knopp.
Tomlinson counterclaimed on a quantum meruit if the agreements were void.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against summary judgment and cross-appeal from Master Price by a litigant in person.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment set aside and the whole matter remitted to the Chancery Division for trial.
enrichment.ratio: Remuneration of a director under a service agreement is not necessarily subject to the same general meeting approval requirement as director remuneration under articles; section 322A may impose liability without knowledge of invalidity, but section 727 relief may still require examination on full facts.
legal_issues: Whether directors' service agreements required shareholder approval
Whether Tomlinson was liable for sums paid to fellow director Knopp
Application of section 322A and section 727 Companies Act 1985
Whether the quantum meruit counterclaim was adequately particularised

confidence.notes: Appellate reversal on a conceded legal point; remaining issues reserved for trial.

notes: Complex Mytravel scheme hearing on bondholder class and section 427 reconstruction; economic interest analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Re Mytravel Group: scheme meetings and bondholder economic interest
key_facts: Mytravel Group Plc applied to convene scheme meetings under section 425 to implement a restructuring involving transfer of the undertaking to Newco.
An ad hoc bondholder committee argued bondholders had sufficient economic interest to vote and that the scheme did not satisfy section 427 reconstruction requirements.
Complex modelling showed large deficits and bondholders' recovery prospects in liquidation were fanciful or nil.
Other creditors supported restructuring over immediate winding up despite present company value appearing insufficient to cover unsubordinated debt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Companies Court application to convene creditors' and members' meetings for a scheme of arrangement and directions on bondholder class composition.
enrichment.outcome: Court concluded bondholders had no economic interest in the company sufficient to require a separate voting class; section 427 analysis and meeting directions followed from that finding.
enrichment.ratio: Where liquidation modelling on untested but supervised assumptions shows no realistic recovery for subordinated bondholders, they may have no economic interest requiring inclusion in a scheme class; hopes of recovery through a restructuring of a successor company do not create present value in the existing company.
legal_issues: Whether bondholders had an economic interest entitling them to vote at scheme meetings
Whether the arrangement fell within section 427 reconstruction provisions
How to treat complex valuation and deficit modelling at the convening stage
Proper composition of creditor classes under section 425
linked_authorities: Re British & Commonwealth Holdings plc [1990] BCLC 240

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; core class-interest conclusion is clear though modelling details are dense.

notes: Case stated appeal on harassment by deliberate failure to control dogs; Leveson J dismissed and criticised route of challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Taffurelli v DPP: harassment by neighbour dispute and dog barking
key_facts: Father and son Gino and Lee Taffurelli were convicted after a seven-day trial of harassment of neighbours Joanna Wyatt and Jacqueline Spencer at adjacent cottages in Malden Rushett.
On 3 May 2003 the family shouted abuse, threw stones and threatened the complainants during a garden confrontation; Gino was also convicted of criminal damage to a car.
The magistrate found deliberate failure to control alsatian and pitbull-type dogs caused excessive early-morning barking through June 2003.
Gino was bailed away from the address from 15 June; findings against him for dog barking were limited to 1 and 8 June.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Kingston Magistrates' Court to the Administrative Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; deliberate failure to control dogs could form part of a course of conduct where the magistrate so found; case stated was an unsuitable vehicle to challenge facts.
enrichment.ratio: A deliberate omission may constitute conduct under the 1997 Act where an owner knowingly fails to control dogs despite complaints, provided the magistrate finds deliberate conduct rather than mere inability to prevent all barking; case stated appeals cannot reinvestigate seven-day trial facts without proper evidential appendices.
legal_issues: Whether failure to control a dog can be conduct for section 1 purposes
Whether a course of conduct was established across May and June incidents
Effect of the addendum clarifying dates and dog ownership findings
Whether prosecution had to mention all evidence in opening

confidence.notes: Legal issue and magistrate's clarified findings are clearly set out.

notes: LPG late delivery damages trial; no available market and reasonable Petrochina settlement upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Contigroup v Glencore: late CFR butane delivery and downstream loss
key_facts: Contichem sold Glencore a CFR butane cargo on the Sunway for delivery at Wenzhou by 10 June 2002 under an exchange contract.
Glencore resold through Glencore International to Chinese retailer Petrochina; the vessel arrived on 15 June carrying butane only, not the mixed propane/butane cargo contracted downstream.
Glencore could not find substitute bulk or pressurised cargoes despite broker efforts; Petrochina settled for an $8/mt abatement totalling $172,899.67 covering delay and related claims.
Contichem withheld that sum in the contractual offset, disputing recoverability of downstream lost-profit damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of price claim with set-off for late delivery damages under an English law CFR LPG contract.
enrichment.outcome: Glencore entitled to damages of $172,899.67 and to set them off against Contichem's balance claim; no available market found for substitute butane.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trader seller knew the buyer would likely resell and no available market existed for substitute goods, foreseeable loss includes reasonable compensation paid to a sub-buyer for lost retail profits caused by delay; settlement referable solely to delay and made after arm's-length negotiation may be recovered.
legal_issues: Whether there was an available market for butane at Wenzhou in early June 2002
Whether Petrochina settlement reflected delay loss or customs duty/propane claims
Whether downstream lost-profit damages were within contractual contemplation
Proper measure of damages absent an available market
linked_authorities: Biggins & Co Ltd v Permanite Ltd [1951] 2 KB 314

confidence.notes: Full trial judgment with detailed findings on market, settlement and damages.

notes: Cocaine importation sentence appeal; section 37 hospital order refused where no causal link to mental illness.

enrichment.short_title: R v N: hospital order refused for schizophrenic cocaine courier
key_facts: A.N. pleaded guilty to importing about 30kg cocaine (15.38kg at 100% purity) hidden in his car at Dover, with estimated street value £1.8m.
Psychiatrists diagnosed schizo-affective disorder and recommended a section 37 hospital order with an available bed.
The judge found no causal link between mental illness and the offence; the appellant acted with eyes open at the direction of Mohammed.
He was sentenced to twelve years' imprisonment with full credit for plea and mitigation for vulnerability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against sentence on certificate of fitness from Canterbury Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; hospital order discretion properly exercised and twelve years not excessive for the quantity involved.
enrichment.ratio: Section 37 confers a discretion even without causal connection between mental disorder and offending, but where a drug importer knowingly commits a serious offence with eyes open and policy requires deterrent focus on the offence, a hospital order will rarely be appropriate; prison treatment and section 47 transfer remain available.
legal_issues: Whether section 37 hospital order should have been made despite unanimous psychiatric recommendation
Relevance of absence of causal link between schizophrenia and importation
Whether twelve years was manifestly excessive for a guilty plea
Application of Howell and related hospital-order authorities
linked_authorities: R v Howell (1985) 7 Cr App R (S) 360
R v Mbatha (1985) 7 Cr App R (S) 373
R v Fairhurst [1996] 1 Cr App R (S) 242

confidence.notes: Clear sentencing principles and psychiatric evidence summarised.

notes: Attorney-General strict liability contempt against Daily Star for naming rape inquiry suspects; £60,000 fine.

enrichment.short_title: Attorney-General v Express Newspapers: Daily Star strict liability contempt
key_facts: The Daily Star uniquely named Newcastle's Titus Bramble and Chelsea/Charlton's Carlton Cole as suspects in an alleged gang rape at the Grosvenor House Hotel on 27 September 2003.
Repeated Attorney-General and Metropolitan Police guidance from 30 September to 22 October warned against naming suspects because identification was in issue.
Proceedings were active; the complainant had not identified the men to police before publication and no charges were ultimately brought.
Express Newspapers conceded systemic failure to heed guidelines and apologised for a bad mistake.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney-General's application for committal for strict liability contempt after leave from the Divisional Court.
enrichment.outcome: Contempt proved beyond reasonable doubt; fine of £60,000 with seven days to pay plus Attorney-General's costs.
enrichment.ratio: Naming possible defendants in a national newspaper when identification is in issue creates a substantial risk of serious prejudice if the complainant did not already know their identities; speculative media clues do not establish prior knowledge; repeated official warnings aggravate the contempt.
legal_issues: Whether publication created a substantial risk of serious impediment or prejudice under section 2(2)
Whether the complainant may already have known identities from other media or internet sources
Admissibility of hearsay in contempt proceedings
Appropriate penalty where guidelines were repeatedly ignored
linked_authorities: Attorney-General v News Group Newspapers Ltd [1987] QB 1

confidence.notes: Findings on prejudice, complainant knowledge and penalty are explicit.
